name: One-pan salmon rice — optimized (אורז עם סלמון במחבת, גרסה מתוקנת)

source.author: Optimized version of one_pan_salmon_rice
source.notes: Corrected version of one_pan_salmon_rice, adopted per user request (only this version goes into rotation; the original stays as reference). Changes: the rice-to-salmon ratio is flipped — rice cut from 2 cups to 1 cup (~185 g dry) with water cut to 1½ cups, and salmon raised to ~550 g; low-sodium soy; no added salt; sesame oil halved to ½ tbsp. Same method. 4 servings. White rice kept so the method/timing stay identical (brown rice is an optional swap, but needs more water and ~35–40 min). Estimate.

ingredients.note: the soy covers it — taste at the end

steps: Sear the salmon skin-side down in a little oil until the skin is crispy, flip and sear the other side; remove when almost cooked.
Toast the rinsed rice in the same pan 1–2 min.
Add 1½ cups water, the low-sodium soy and garlic (no salt) and stir.
Lay the salmon on the rice, cover, bring to a boil on medium, then cook on low 12–15 min.
Turn off the heat and leave covered 10 more min.
Flake the salmon, add plenty of spring onion, the sesame oil and sesame seeds, and mix. Keep the crispy skin on top or remove it.

batch_totals.note: Whole pan (4 servings), optimized. Vs the original (per serving ~605 kcal / 26 g protein / 77 g carb / ~830 mg sodium): ~80 kcal less, +7 g protein, carbs roughly halved, sodium halved, and about 1.5x the omega-3 and vitamin D. The extra fat is almost all salmon fat (omega-3), not added oil.

him.verdict: Flipping the ratio turns this from a rice dish with some salmon into a salmon dish with some rice: ~33 g protein and only ~40 g carbs for ~526 kcal, with roughly 2.5 g omega-3 and ~700 IU vitamin D per serving — two of your top sperm-priority micros in big amounts. Sodium is halved (low-sodium soy, no added salt). Fat is still ~25 g, but nearly all of it is salmon's own omega-3-rich fat. Fibre is low (white rice), so add a green side.
flags: ~33 g protein / ~40 g carbs per serving (was 26 g / 77 g)
~2.5 g omega-3 + ~700 IU vitamin D per serving (sperm micros)
suggested_mods: Serve with a green vegetable side (broccoli, edamame) for fibre
Optional: brown rice for fibre (needs more water and ~35–40 min cook)

her_preconception.verdict: Excellent for her: more low-mercury salmon per serving means more DHA and vitamin D — both key for fetal brain development — plus selenium and B12, with lower sodium than the original. Fully cooked by steaming on the rice; confirm the salmon is opaque throughout. Pair with greens for folate.
prenatal_highlights: high DHA/omega-3 + vitamin D (salmon) — fetal brain development
low-mercury fish; selenium + B12; lower sodium; fully cooked

safety_advisories.note: Salmon finishes cooking on the rice — check it's fully opaque and flakes before serving.
safety_advisories.swap: a few extra minutes covered if the centre is translucent

suggested_mods: Serve with a green vegetable side for folate + vitamin C

adopted_note: Adopted 2026-11-10 (corrected/optimized version only — the original one_pan_salmon_rice stays as reference). Per serving (of 4, ~265 g): ~526 kcal, 33 g protein, 39.6 g carb, 25.1 g fat, ~2.5 g omega-3, ~420 mg sodium. him 8 / her 9. Standing spec: 1 cup rice + 1½ cups water, ~550 g salmon, low-sodium soy, no added salt, ½ tbsp sesame oil. Serve with greens.
cooking_guide: Pat the salmon skin completely dry and start it skin-down in a hot, lightly oiled pan; press gently for the first 30 sec so it stays flat and crisps evenly. Don't move it until it releases on its own.
Pull the salmon while the centre is still slightly translucent — it finishes cooking as it steams on top of the rice.
Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear and drain well, so the grains stay separate.
With half the rice, keep the water at 1½ cups — don't use the original 3 cups or it'll be soupy.
Once it boils, drop to the lowest heat and don't lift the lid; then rest 10 min covered off the heat.
Add spring onion, sesame oil and sesame only at the end. Taste before adding any salt — with soy you usually won't need it.
